newsitem.title: AUSTRIA: Analysts cautious on Bank Austria bid for CA.
newsitem.headline: Analysts cautious on Bank Austria bid for CA.

text.p: A possible bid by Bank Austria for rival Creditanstalt-Bankverein could give Austrian banking a much needed shake-up but analysts doubted on Wednesday it would trigger necessary reforms.

The supervisory board of Bank Austria, controlled by the City of Vienna, was due to meet at 1500 GMT to discuss lodging a bid for privatisation candidate Creditanstalt ahead of a December 16 deadline.

But analysts said the marriage of Bank Austria, backed by the ruling Social Democrats, and the nation's most traditional bank, a bastion of junior coalition partner the conservative People's Party, would be far from harmonious.
"Looking at the way these two banks operate, I can see a Bank Austria takeover becoming a disaster," said an analyst who declined to be named.
The People's Party has publicly backed an EA-Generali led bid for Creditanstalt. The EA-Generali consortium is made up of financiers and industrialists allied to the conservatives.
"In the end the whole thing will be a political decision," said Victoria Maxwell of James Capel in London.

Bank Austria, with a market share of 12.8 percent in terms of total assets, and Creditanstalt, with around 12 percent, are market leaders in Austria's overcrowded and politically polarised banking sector.

"This is a logical step towards consolidating Austrian banking but there could be a problem of integration. They are two very different houses with very different management cultures," said Gerhard Auer, an analyst at ICE Securities in London.

He noted a takeover would create one dominant Austrian bank and an institution that would be a major European player. Bank Austria's traditional role as a savings bank would complement Creditanstalt's commercial banking expertise.
"But they would have to merge their investment banking activities, bringing a lot of job losses, and they would have to shut a lot of branches."

James Capel's Maxwell doubted that promised synergies would bear fruit, given Austria's banking culture. Bank Austria had scored only limited success in integrating GiroCredit into its operations after a 1994 takeover, she noted.
"I see few synergy gains...Bank Austria will want a greater critical mass to be a presence in Europe. (A takeover) will make it a bigger organisation but not necessarily more competitive," she said.
Austrian analysts were reluctant to discuss the possible sale publicly but in private they voiced the same doubts.
"It is a question of speed. Initially a lot of energy will be spent on developing a new structure and that could be a handicap for quite some time," one said.

Market watchers forecast that a Bank Austria and Creditanstalt link-up could also draw scrutiny from the European Union, wary of one institution dominating the Austrian market. -- Vienna Newsroom, 43-1-53112-258
